highlights.title: Keurig Alta Brewer Review: Brand-New Tech, Classically Good Coffee
highlights.summary: This multifaceted home coffee brewer and its new AltaRounds will make you rethink everything you know about Keurig machines.
body: The Keurig Alta looks like something straight out of a design convention. It almost looks like spaceship decor with its curved white lines and sleek components (it also comes in black and stainless steel). Whereas some inexpensive Keurigs —the kind that sell for $50 during shopping holidays—can feel cheap and plasticky, this machine feels high-end from top to bottom. The cup holder is metal, the cup and whisk for the steam wand are magnetic, and the reservoir bin is slim and reversible. Both drip trays tuck away seamlessly without adding extra bulk.

The top of the machine has two compartments. On the right side, you'll find the standard Keurig K-Cup basket, with the typical needle at the bottom to pierce the cup. On the left, though, is a new compartment for the brand-new Keurig AltaRounds ( $11 for a box of 8). These little pucks are the latest in Keurig's coffee technology and are like nothing I've seen before. The whole package comes at a high price point, but compared to in-home espresso makers, it's not unreasonable.

highlights.title: 60 Years Later, the Best 'Peanuts' Quote of All Time Still Doesn't Get the Credit it Deserves
highlights.summary: One of the best examples comes from a Feb. 3, 1966, comic strip in which Lucy mocks him for volunteering for a school spelling bee. Charlie Brown’s response contains some of the best advice Schulz ever put on the page. Sixty years later, it’s still something we can all stand to remember.
body: Charlie Brown has plenty of reasons to stop trying. In Charles Schulz’s Peanuts, his baseball games end in defeat, his kite gets stuck in a tree, and trusting Lucy to hold a football always ends painfully. Yet he keeps coming back. For all his worrying, Charlie Brown has a stubborn streak of hope that makes even his smallest acts of courage worth rooting for.

Schulz had announced his retirement two months earlier due to several strokes and advancing colorectal cancer, and he’d created his last strip shortly after he made the announcement. While Schulz knew he was dying, he couldn’t have known two months in advance the exact day he would die and that he’d essentially penned his own obituary by having his last comic run just one day after his death.

The timing was auspicious and perhaps even profound, which was fitting for a man with such a profound impact on American culture. Over his 50-year career, Schulz gave us nearly 18,000 Peanuts comics. Some were sweet, some were funny, and some were incredibly deep, like this one from February 3, 1966, which contains Schulz’s best-ever quote, a high bar for such a prolific talent.

highlights.title: Sanjay Gupta, Indian Director of ‘Kaante’ and ‘Zinda,’ Dies at 59
highlights.summary: Indian filmmaker Sanjay Gupta, whose credits include the crime thriller “Kaante,” the gangster saga “Shootout at Wadala” and the Hrithik Roshan-starring “Kaabil,” has died following a fall at his Mumbai residence on Oct. 30. He was 59, according to the Press Trust of India.
body: Police in Mumbai’s Versova neighborhood have filed an accidental death report. Deputy Commissioner of Police Purushottam Karad told the Free Press Journal that members of Gupta’s family were sleeping when the incident occurred and became aware of it the following morning. “The family has not raised any suspicion or lodged a complaint,” Karad said.

Gupta was a prominent exponent of the glossy, action-driven Hindi-language crime thriller, bringing a visual sensibility heavily indebted to Hollywood to an industry traditionally dominated by melodrama and musicals. His career behind the camera began with “Aatish: Feel the Fire” in 1994, featuring Sanjay Dutt and Aditya Pancholi. He subsequently directed “Ram Shastra,” “Jung” and “Khauff,” developing an enduring professional relationship with Dutt that extended across 10 films, including projects Gupta produced.

highlights.title: Are Memories Transferable? Meet the Scientists Replicating an Infamous Study to Find Out
highlights.summary: In the 1960’s, an odd experiment showed planarian worms could transfer memories by consuming each other. It was a sensational finding—that is until the worms stopped learning.
body: It was the dead of winter in Boston. The surface of the Charles River was frozen solid. But Zachary Kelso braved the biting cold to finally put to rest a mystery that has haunted neuroscience labs for over half a century.

To do that, Kelso, a research assistant in the Harvard lab of the neuroscientist Sam Gershman, needed some worms. Specifically, planarians: arrow-headed flatworms, which are among the simplest creatures to possess a brain and a nervous system with bilateral symmetry like ours. Normally, labs order these widely used model organisms from biological supply companies. But the mail-order worms weren’t up to snuff. So Gershman had dispatched Kelso to the Charles’ icy banks to catch some wild ones. “I thought, ‘I’m going to look crazy because I’m using a hammer to beat through the ice,’” Kelso recalled. “So I wore the more business end of business casual.”

highlights.title: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
highlights.summary: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable.
body: The new control will allow publishers to apply their AI training preferences across multiple crawlers.

The shared “policy token” signal is proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). It will live within a website’s robots.txt file, which has long signaled which web crawlers can and can’t scrape a site — whether for search indexing, archiving, or AI training. Currently, sites have to signal their AI training preferences separately to each AI company.

The announcement comes as publishers grapple with the continuing influx of AI crawlers scraping their sites and feeding their content into AI models. Some companies and organizations have attempted to combat unauthorized scraping, with the Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard giving publishers the ability to charge crawlers that visit their sites, and Cloudflare blocking AI crawlers by default.

highlights.title: Nintendo’s Biggest Game of the Year Isn't What You Think It Is
highlights.summary: This is the time of year when Nintendo's global marketing departments start limbering up and doing stretches for a big mass-market retail push. Nintendo UK launched a wholesome and emotive campaign this week, seemingly trying to one-up Nintendo Australia's legendary sad Zelda dad campaign for Tears…
body: It's been a quiet week in Switch world (give or take an Indie World showcase), sandwiched between the twin pillars of Nintendo's fall — Nintendo Switch Sports Resort and the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Time to reflect; time to work on the timing of my table tennis backhand.

Titled "Back to Me," the ad features a despondent young student calling home; it seems like he's just been dumped. His dad invites him back for a family meal, and obviously he plays Ocarina on the train. I assumed a family session of Switch Sports Resort would feature next… but no. Instead, he and his sister make a Mii of his dad in Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. He returns to uni, thoroughly cheered up, where he plays more Tomodachi Life with his sister over GameChat.

Tomodachi Life came out in April for the original Switch. It doesn't even have a Switch 2 Edition (yet). If Nintendo UK wanted to throw the spotlight on a game with casual appeal, GameChat support, and family avatars for their storyline, Resort was sitting right there. What gives?

highlights.title: Mobile’s Halloween tricks and treats: Clash of Clans, Talking Tom, Monopoly Go, Fortnite and more
highlights.summary: Halloween is almost here and with it comes a reliable range of mobile games tapping into the spooky season. In-game events, cosmetics and more can be found across all kinds of genres, as can a sizeable helping of pumpkins, witches and autumnal scenery.
body: Whether it’s Pokémon Sleep turning towards nightmarish ghosts like Gengar, or a growing cast of horror characters in Fortnite, there’s a good chance one game or other will land a scare.

This year, Epic Games, Zynga, The Pokémon Company, Scopely, Intelligent Systems and even The New York Times are among those dressing up their games for the occasion. Many of them also recently landed among our Top 50 Mobile Game Makers of 2026.

The aptly named Fortnitemares event has brought a month of cursed content to Epic Games’ flagship, tapping into a lineup of characters like Freddy Krueger, Ghost Face and Freddy Fazbear. In fact, characters from the Five Nights at Freddy’s universe are going all-in on the fright factor, with their outfits able to show battle damage.

Other IPs trickling in throughout October have included Hollow Knight, Slender Man, Beetlejuice and Obsession. Meanwhile, gameplay has seen players firing pumpkin rockets, teleporting around and dropping into Reload’s Nitemare Island.

body: The Tokyo International Film Festival ’s Tokyo Talk program presented a masterclass with Zeze Takahisa, director of the festival’s opening film, “Sukiyaki.”

Pink films screened in specialized theaters for an exclusively male audience, and directors had to insert a bed scene every 10 minutes or so. “I’ve always been pretty firm in my convictions,” said Zeze. “Starting from the early 1990s the culture shifted and I had more freedom to say what I wanted. That kind of thing was important to me.”
At the time, Zeze was interested in stories about female criminals. “It’s just different from the male perspective,” he said. “The motives behind the crimes and so on. I found it fascinating.”

Scripted by Zeze, “Extracurricular Activity: Rape” was about delinquent high school girls who hang out at Tokyo’s Haneda Airport and battle the yakuza. Zeze gave it the “private” title “Go to Haneda and You Will See Kids Dressed Like Pirates Ready to Attack.”

highlights.title: ‘We’re looking at a 30-year run’: UK pair aim to complete world’s most complex board game
highlights.summary: Decades from now, friends may become first people known to have finished The Campaign for North Africa. “We have had a six-turn practice run. It took about 18 months,” said Andy Taeger, with what seemed like a chuckle as he contemplated playing the world’s most complicated board game.
body: “Based on that, we are looking at a 20- to 30-year run for the full game,” said his gaming partner James Purcell. “We’ve come to terms with it.”
The Guardian joined the pair in a Newcastle front room on Friday as they prepared to start an insane odyssey, playing the legendarily knotty war game The Campaign for North Africa.

If they finish it – and that, subject to the events of the next two to three decades, is the intention – they will become the first people known to have completed a game so vast, detailed and time-consuming that it has achieved mythical status in board gaming communities. It is a holy grail.

Purcell, 29, is a mental health worker from Wallsend, Taeger, 30, a software developer from Gosforth. They’re happy to be called geeks. They met about 10 years ago and realised straight away that they had a connection.

highlights.summary: I’ve never been a morning person. This bedside gadget is the only thing that’s ever changed that.
body: With darker days ahead, waking up in the morning can be rough. If you never feel rested when your alarm goes off, a sunrise alarm clock could change your life. The gradually brightening light signals that it’s time to wake up instead of beeps and harsh, unnatural tones. I’m a chronic snooze-button kind of gal, and I’ve found a sunrise clock, or wake-up light, incredibly helpful for getting up when I need to and for supporting a healthier circadian rhythm. Plus, it’s much harder to ignore than a phone alarm that I can simply snooze.

If you want to face dark winter mornings by waking up more gently and naturally, using a sunrise alarm clock might just improve your mood. We recommend the newly released Hatch Sleep Clock if you want a sunrise alarm and sleep tracker in one machine, as well as a personal favorite, the Lumie Bodyclock Luxe 700FM.

highlights.title: MIT affiliates named 2026 Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Fellows
highlights.summary: Five MIT faculty members and two additional alumni are honored with fellowships to advance research on beneficial AI.
body: Five MIT faculty members and two additional alumni were recently named to the 2026 cohort of AI2050 Fellows. The honor is announced annually by Schmidt Sciences, Eric and Wendy Schmidt’s philanthropic initiative that aims to accelerate scientific innovation.

Conceived and co-chaired by Eric Schmidt and James Manyika, AI2050 is a philanthropic initiative aimed at helping to solve hard problems in artificial intelligence. Within their research, each fellow will contend with the central motivating question of AI2050: “It’s 2050. AI has turned out to be hugely beneficial to society. What happened? What are the most important problems we solved and the opportunities and possibilities we realized to ensure this outcome?”
MIT alumni Irene Chen PhD '22 and Allison Z. Koenecke '14 as well as former postdoc Juan Carlos Perdomo were also named AI2050 Early Career Fellows.

highlights.title: What we've been playing - "I've been intrigued by horrible images of live-action sequences for weeks"
highlights.summary: Happy Halloween! Are you scared? I am: I'm in a theatre play that opens next week and we're not ready yet. I'm also off to a ghost stories evening at the theatre tonight; I've had a few people there tell me, with faces as straight as a ruler, of their eerie encounters.
body: I was in a two-hander there, a play with only two people in it, and I got to the changing room one evening to see a concerned look on the face of the other person in the show. "Have you only just got here?" he asked. "Yes," I said in response. And at this, he blanched. He's a gruff sort of fellow with a streetwise sensibility: not a person I would associate with being easily scared. But he was. "I was just talking to you," he said. "You made the curtain move as you walked past." I remember the hairs on my arms and neck standing up, and I haven't been as confident sitting in that dressing room alone since.

But back to games! This, as you know, is our regular feature where we talk about what we've been playing this week. This week, Marie cooks with Death; Connor revisits a game that terrified him as a teenager; and Bertie is a little bit disappointed by a new indie horror.

But enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago (it happens). And now onward!

highlights.title: Japan’s Film Funds Look Beyond Production Committees to Build New Financing Models
highlights.summary: Japan’s production committee system, in which a group of companies jointly finance a film and share its rights, has helped spread risk across the industry. But it can also cap budgets at what the industry itself can raise, make it harder for overseas investors to take part and slow decisions when…
body: “Film Funds in Japan: What Works, What Doesn’t, and What Comes Next” featured Kii Muneyuki, CEO and producer of K2 Pictures, which works with filmmakers including Kore-eda Hirokazu, Miike Takashi and Nishikawa Miwa; Ibe Tomonobu, CEO of Questry, a Tokyo startup that uses digital securities to fund anime and other Japanese content; Nakagawa Keita, managing director at MUFG Bank; and Motoyanagi Yusuke, partner at law firm Nishimura & Asahi.

Kii presented K2P Film Fund I as one example of a new structure. The fund closed in February at about JPY5 billion ($32 million) and aims to back around 50 films over seven years. It is a blind pool, meaning investors commit money before the films are chosen. Its investors include MUFG, the Development Bank of Japan and other financial institutions and companies, and a greenlight committee oversees project approvals. Kii said five films had been released in theaters in 2026.
points: Japan’s production committee system, in which a group of companies jointly finance a film and share its rights, has helped spread risk across the industry.

Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions in debt financing for AI cloud provider Nscale’s planned Anthropic data center in West Virginia, The Information reported Thursday. Bloomberg later corroborated the report. Anthropic has signed a $44.6 billion contract for the project’s first building alone, according to Nscale’s IPO filing. In essence, the chipmaker would be co-signing a customer’s loans, a sign of how hard the AI industry is working to keep its buildout plans afloat as investors grow jittery about the amounts of money involved.

The proposed arrangement would help Nscale secure financing for the electricity and construction costs of its West Virginia campus. Under what’s known as a residual value guarantee, Nvidia would step in if Nscale defaulted on construction payments, temporarily take over the facility, and help find a buyer and new tenant, according to The Information.

highlights.title: CBS's Legendary 156-Episode Sci-Fi Anthology Series is Officially Free to Watch on Streaming
highlights.summary: In the realm of science fiction, Star Wars and Star Trek are generally considered to be the two biggest and most important franchises of all time. If you’re purely talking about profitability, that’s correct; those two have dominated TV and film for decades.
body: You can currently watch The Twilight Zone for free with ads on Pluto TV, Fandango, and The Roku Channel.

Debuting in 1959, The Twilight Zone ran for five seasons on CBS, totaling 156 episodes. It was created by Rod Serling, a television pioneer who sought to expand what had been seen on television throughout the 1950s, much of which was taped plays and multi-camera sitcoms like I Love Lucy. To do this, he created The Twilight Zone, a single-camera anthology series where each episode would operate like a little movie (for most of its run, the show ran for a half-hour, but season 4 tried out an hour-long format before switching back to half-hours for season 5).

While every episode of The Twilight Zone has its own characters and premise, it often explores science fiction subjects like time travel and aliens, as well as horror staples like ghosts and possessed dolls. But that was just the surface-level stuff, as many of the deeper messages in the series tackled things like prejudice, loneliness, morality, and regret.
points: In the realm of science fiction, Star Wars and Star Trek are generally considered to be the two biggest and most important franchises of all time.

highlights.title: Tim Dowling: having a tortoise reminds you that life is long
highlights.summary: My wife got ours when she was eight, and he came to live with us soon after we got married. I don’t remember anything about that in the vows. It is the first truly bleak day of autumn – the sky is a deep grey and a steady drizzle is falling.
body: Except it isn’t, quite, as a few hours later the cloud begins to break up and a shaft of watery sunlight reaches the brick step just outside my office shed. When I open the door to let in the warm afternoon air, I find the tortoise sitting there.

There aren’t many pets that allow you to forget their existence for any length of time. The cat reminds me that I have a cat twice a day. The dog will not let me forget I have a dog for half an hour. But it has been at least a week since it even occurred to me that I have a tortoise.
“All good?” I say. The tortoise winds its neck anticlockwise, so it can fix me with its right eye.

Certain experiences – raising children, say, or stepping into the path of a bus – remind you that life is short. But many other experiences remind you that it’s long – mostly things breaking, and then breaking again. I have measured out my life in dual-function push-button kitchen tap spray head replacements – they last, on average, about three years, and according to my order history, I’m on my fourth one.

highlights.title: White Dwarfs Aren’t Just White. Scientists Discover Dying Stars Turning Pink and Green
highlights.summary: Astronomers find that a white dwarf’s density and the kind of material it absorbed from its surroundings can produce a rainbow of shades in the star’s atmosphere.
body: The realm of stars resembles a fairy tale. In it, we find giants, supergiants, and also many dwarfs. Rather like the flames of a fire, most stars’ colors are based on temperature. Cooler stars look orange, sun-like stars appear white, and the hottest ones shine light blue. However, there are exceptions, and astronomers have recently discovered some among the class of stars known as white dwarfs.

At the end of their lives, stars with a mass similar to the sun expand and turn into red giants. Subsequently, they shed their gaseous envelope, creating a planetary nebula that we can admire through telescopes. In place of the star, a white dwarf remains—a highly condensed object the approximate volume of the Earth but the mass of the sun.

Initially, white dwarfs have extremely high temperatures, and so the first ones discovered shone from white to light blue. That’s how they got their name. But according to a new study published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments, the world of white dwarfs is actually far more colorful—with some stars turning pink, green, and even purple.

highlights.title: Q&A: Hey AI, who should I vote for this year?
highlights.summary: MIT professors Adam Berinsky and Chara Podimata discuss a new project to track how AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.
body: People are peppering artificial intelligence chatbots everyday with questions, but when it comes to politics and the looming 2026 U.S. midterm elections, what role are AI platforms playing? Could an AI chatbot sway a voter to switch parties or re-examine their political beliefs?

MIT researchers have built a new dashboard, called the LLM Election Observatory, to examine, in real-time, how popular AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 midterm elections. The team behind the dashboard — led by Professor Adam Berinsky, Assistant Professor Chara Podimata, and Professor Charles Stewart III — has extensive experience studying voting and election administration, AI and misinformation, and how AI systems are impacting human decision making. In an effort to better understand how AI is shaping the election, they designed the dashboard to simulate how individuals across the country communicate with chatbots.

highlights.title: ‘Apologies for any confusion!’: how to write the perfect passive-aggressive email
highlights.summary: In a survey, ‘just to be clear’ came out as the most loathed phrase. But I think I can do better. A new contender for the most passive-aggressive email phrase has emerged.
body: If you ask me, these all verge on actual aggressive. Imagine saying “just to be clear” out loud to another person: that’s a conversational poke in the ribs, isn’t it? It’s the kind of thing you unleash 10 minutes into an ill-tempered wrangle with your home insurance company about inflated renewal premiums. “Kindly note” is even worse – it’s a phrase from an angry message on the office kitchen wall about microwave abuse.

No, we can do better than that, or at least I – a person whose own spouse frequently describes her as unpleasantly passive-aggressive – can. Let me explain: an exchange of professional passive-aggressive emails is a ritual as intricately coded as a Belle Epoque duel and it demands the appearance of great politeness. Your message needs to read, on its surface, as exquisitely helpful and friendly, while leaving every cc and bcc on the thread in no doubt as to it what it really is: an epistolary shanking.
